segments.say: The bill is paid at last, and the five friends are pulling on coats by the door, still smiling. Someone makes a small comment about the teapot and there's a ripple of fresh giggles. Nadia notices that she has laughed more in the last three hours than in the whole of the previous week. And almost none of it, she realises, was at anything she'd call a joke.

Provine's notebooks suggested that laughter is mainly social. But noticing a pattern isn't the same as testing it. So the next step was to ask people to keep track of their own laughter, and to note exactly where they were, and who they were with, each time they laughed. That's exactly what Provine did next, with a colleague named Kenneth Fischer.

In a study published in 1989 in the journal Ethology, students carried small logbooks for a week. Every time they laughed, smiled or talked, they wrote it down, along with whether they were alone or with other people, and whether anything like television or reading was involved. It was simple, a little tedious, and very revealing.

show.what: Laughing, smiling and talking: relation to sleeping and social context in humans

segments.say: The difference was enormous. The students laughed about thirty times more often when they were with other people than when they were alone. Smiling and talking showed the same social pattern, but laughter was the most social of all. And many of the laughs that did happen alone came while watching, reading or listening to something, a kind of company of its own.

show.title: More laughter with others than alone
show.label: in Provine and Fischer's logbooks

segments.say: You can test this gently against your own life. Think back over the past day or two. How many times did you laugh out loud when you were completely alone, with no screen, no book, no message from anyone? For most of us, the answer is very few. We might smile at a thought, but the full laugh tends to wait for company.

That's part of why the teapot lid was so funny at Nadia's table. The lid itself wasn't much. But it fell in front of four people she loves, people who share twenty years of jokes and memories with her, people whose laughter she can hear and see and feel. Laughter grows in company like a fire grows with air.

The same thing shows up early in life. In a study published in 2018, Caspar Addyman and colleagues showed short funny cartoons to young children, aged about two and a half to four. Some watched alone, some with another child, and some in a group. The researchers then counted the laughs and smiles on each child's face.

show.what: Social facilitation of laughter and smiles in preschool children

segments.say: The children laughed far more when they watched with another child than when they watched alone, even though the cartoon was exactly the same. Being with someone else didn't change the joke. It changed the child. Even before they can tie their own shoelaces, human beings seem to treat laughter as something best done together.

A row of coats and scarves hanging on hooks beside a restaurant door, with warm light inside and rain on the glass. It's the small, ordinary moment at the end of a good evening, when people linger by the door, not quite ready to go. Often, some of the warmest laughter of the whole evening happens right here, in the doorway, between goodbyes.

Other researchers asked adults to keep laughter diaries too. In a study published in 1999, Rod Martin and Nicholas Kuiper had people record every laugh over several days. People laughed many times a day, mostly in conversation, and the amounts varied a great deal between individuals. Some laughed often. Some much less. Very few laughs came from formal jokes.

show.where: Humor: International Journal of Humor Research, 1999

segments.say: Put these diary studies side by side and a consistent picture forms. We laugh many times a day. Mostly with other people. Mostly in ordinary conversation. Rarely at formal, told jokes. And with big differences from one person to the next. Nadia, with her famous laugh, is probably somewhere near the top of that range, and that's fine.

show.title: What the diaries keep showing
items: We laugh many times a day

segments.say: If laughter is so tied to company, it seems likely that its main job is social. One way to put it is that laughter is a signal. It tells the people around us something about our mood and our intentions: that we're relaxed, that we're playing, that we're on the same side. And signals, by their nature, need someone to receive them.

A quick word of caution, though. Diaries and logbooks rely on people noticing and remembering their own laughs, and we're not always good at that. Small laughs are easy to miss, and some people may record more carefully than others. So the exact numbers should be taken loosely. But the overall pattern, that we laugh far more with others, has held up again and again.

Provine summed up his work in a simple idea, which we can paraphrase like this. Laughter is not primarily about humour. It's about relationships. Humour is just one of the things that sets it off. The deeper job of a laugh is to connect us, to smooth things over, to show we're friends, and to make a group feel like a group.

show.text: Laughter is not primarily about humour, but about social relationships

segments.say: Out on the pavement, the rain has eased to a fine drizzle. The friends hug, promise not to leave it so long next time, and set off in different directions. Nadia waves goodbye to Tom, who is still shaking his head about the teapot. As she turns towards home, she's grinning, and she isn't even sure why. Laughter has a way of lingering.

But something else from the evening is nagging at her. The couple at the next table. They didn't see the teapot lid. They didn't know any of the friends. And yet they laughed too. How does laughter jump like that, from one table to another, between complete strangers? That's our next question.
